subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: At the bus stand, a young man in a torn black hoodie with tattoos on his arm and earphones sat beside Joseph. Joseph gripped his bag and shifted along the bench. His hand checked the wallet in his pocket twice. Then the wallet slipped onto the ground without Joseph noticing. The young man tapped his shoulder. "Bhai, your wallet." Joseph took it, face hot, and mumbled thanks. "Karthik," the stranger said, and went back to his tune. Joseph thought: why did I decide all that from a hoodie? It was a cold, honest thought, not a whipping. On the bus Joseph promised to catch the next assumption sooner, and asked Karthik which stop was his.

qa.q: What did the young man say when he tapped Joseph's shoulder?
qa.a: The young man said, Bhai, your wallet.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel gripping the bag, and later?
qa.a: Uneasy and suspicious at first, then embarrassed; the face went hot after the wallet was returned.

qa.q: What was healthy about how Joseph dealt with the bias?
qa.a: Joseph noticed the assumption honestly, without harsh self-punishment, and decided to catch it sooner.

qa.q: How might Karthik have seen Joseph's gripped bag?
qa.a: As unfair suspicion, possibly hurtful, though Karthik still returned the wallet.

grounding: A young adult realises he assumed a stranger would behave a certain way from dress, and notices the bias honestly.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: On a tram in Lisbon, Rosa moved her bag to the far side when a man in a long coat and scarf sat beside her, speaking low on the phone in a language she couldn't place. Her stomach tightened. Each stop felt long. Then a small boy across the aisle dropped a mitten. The man picked it up, smiled and handed it back. Then he turned to Rosa. "You dropped your ticket," he said, holding it out. "I'm Tuan, by the way." Rosa thanked him and felt her cheeks warm. What did I actually see? A coat and a language. She moved the bag back onto her lap, said, "Nice to meet you," and made a note to notice sooner next time.

qa.q: What did Rosa move to the far side?
qa.a: Rosa moved her bag to the far side.

qa.q: What was Rosa feeling when her stomach tightened, and what did she later notice?
qa.a: Anxious and wary; later she noticed she had judged from a coat and a language.

qa.q: How could Rosa treat this without self-punishment?
qa.a: Name the assumption honestly, move the bag back, be friendly, and try to notice sooner next time.

qa.q: How might Tuan have felt seeing the bag moved away?
qa.a: Possibly hurt or uncomfortable, though Tuan still helped by returning the ticket.

grounding: A young adult realises she assumed a stranger would behave a certain way from clothing and language, and notices it honestly.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: Uma, sit, your Uday Thatha will tell you something about himself that's not so nice. I was twenty, on the Madras bus to college. A man got on in a torn lungi, smelling of fish, and sat next to me. I pulled my bag closer to my chest. I was sure he'd try to steal it. My whole body went stiff. Then the conductor dropped a ticket book, and this man picked it up and read out the page numbers in perfect English to help. He was a teacher, going to the market for his mother. I felt hot in the face. I had judged him by his clothes in three seconds. I didn't punish myself for years, but I didn't forget either. After that, whenever I felt that stiffness, I asked myself: what do I actually know? Often, nothing.

qa.q: How did the man help the conductor?
qa.a: He picked up the dropped ticket book and read out the page numbers in perfect English.

qa.q: What was young Uday feeling when the man sat next to him?
qa.a: He felt suspicious and uneasy, his body stiffening and holding his bag close.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Thatha's story, and what did he do with it?
qa.a: Seeing the man help the conductor showed him he had judged by clothes; afterwards he asked himself what he actually knew whenever he felt that stiffness.

qa.q: How might the man in the lungi have felt if he noticed Uday clutching his bag?
qa.a: He may have felt hurt or tired of being treated as a thief because of his clothes.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who notices he assumed a stranger would behave a certain way because of dress, and names the bias honestly without self-punishment.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: The night bus from Manali broke down near a dhaba at 2 a.m., in pouring rain, and the driver said it would take an hour. Lokesh, twenty, got off and stood under the tin roof. A young woman with a shaved head, tattoos up both arms and a heavy leather jacket stood nearby. Lokesh moved a step away without thinking. He expected her to be rude or trouble. Then an old man slipped on the wet steps. She was there first, holding his elbow, then asked the dhaba owner for a dry chair. "I'm Pema," she said later, handing Lokesh a cup of tea. "Nurse in Delhi." Lokesh took the tea and felt uneasy about that step he'd taken. He didn't make a big speech to himself. He just noticed it: tattoos, rude. Where did that come from? The bus coughed back to life.

qa.q: What was Pema's job?
qa.a: A nurse in Delhi.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel when Pema handed him tea?
qa.a: Lokesh felt uneasy and a little embarrassed about the step he had taken away from her.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do with his mistake that was healthy?
qa.a: He noticed the assumption honestly and asked where it came from, without punishing himself or making a big speech.

qa.q: What might it be like for Pema when strangers step away from her?
qa.a: It may feel tiring and a bit hurtful, being judged by her tattoos and jacket before she has said anything.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who notices he assumed a stranger would behave badly based on dress, and names the bias honestly without self-punishment.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage: On her first week at the Chennai software office, Ganga was paired with Lakshmi, who wore a simple cotton sari, oiled plait and a small bindi, and spoke softly in Tamil to the security guard. Ganga, twenty-one, caught herself thinking: she won't know the new testing tool; I'll have to carry her. When the build broke on Thursday, Ganga panicked. Lakshmi read the log for thirty seconds, said, "Missing dependency, line forty," and fixed it. Ganga felt her face go warm. She hadn't said anything unkind, but she'd thought it. At lunch she admitted to herself, not with drama, that she'd judged Lakshmi by her clothes and her quietness. She didn't beat herself up. She just asked Lakshmi, "Can you show me how you read logs so fast?" Lakshmi smiled and pulled up a chair.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi say was wrong with the build?
qa.a: "Missing dependency, line forty."

qa.q: How did Ganga feel when Lakshmi fixed the build?
qa.a: Ganga felt embarrassed, her face going warm, because she had assumed Lakshmi would need carrying.

qa.q: What did Ganga do well after noticing her bias?
qa.a: She admitted it to herself honestly without beating herself up, and then asked Lakshmi to teach her, turning the moment into respect.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have felt when Ganga asked to learn from her?
qa.a: Lakshmi probably felt pleased and respected, and perhaps unaware she had ever been underestimated.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who notices she assumed a colleague's skill from dress and manner, and names the bias honestly without self-punishment.

subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
passage:
"Wasim, you're home early."
"Class got cancelled. Why do you look like that?"
"Like what?"
"Like you swallowed a lemon, Afreen."
"Okay. On the metro there was this guy. Ripped jeans, tattoos up his neck, music blasting. I moved my bag to my other side and stood by the door."
"And?"
"My purse fell out when I got off. He ran after me across the platform to give it back. Said, 'Didi, your stuff.' Then he just left."
"So he was nice."
"He was nice. And I'd already decided he was a thief. Just from his clothes. That's what's bothering me."
"You're making a face like you robbed a bank."
"My stomach dropped the second I saw him, Wasim. I didn't even think."
"But you're thinking now. Ammi always says the first thought comes by itself; the second one is yours."
"Yeah. Next time I'll catch the first one."

qa.q: What did the man say when he gave back the purse?
qa.a: He said, "Didi, your stuff," and then he just left.

qa.q: What is Afreen feeling after she gets home, and why?
qa.a: She feels ashamed and uneasy, because she had decided the man was a thief from his clothes alone, and he turned out to be kind.

qa.q: What does Afreen plan to do next time, and why is it a good start?
qa.a: She plans to catch her first thought when it comes; spotting a snap judgment honestly, without beating herself up, leaves room for a fairer second thought.

qa.q: How might the man on the platform have felt if he had noticed Afreen moving her bag away?
qa.a: He might have felt judged or hurt, yet he still ran after her with the purse, which shows how little his clothes said about him.

grounding: Shows a young adult catching her snap judgment of a stranger from his dress and noticing it honestly without harsh self-blame.
